section.title: Released from the Law
section.sectionRationale: Having shown that believers have died to sin and been freed to serve God, Paul now turns to their relationship to the law. Using the analogy of marriage, he argues that the law binds a person only as long as he lives. As a widow is released from the marriage law when her husband dies, so believers, having died to the law through the body of Christ, are released from it to belong to another, to the risen Christ, so as to bear fruit to God and serve in the new way of the Spirit rather than the old way of the written code.
section.thesis: The law holds authority over a person only during life; and because believers have died to the law through the body of Christ, they are released from it and joined to the risen Christ, so that they bear fruit to God and serve in the new way of the Spirit, not the old way of the letter.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the principle, the law binds only during life; the marriage analogy, a widow released to marry another; and the application, you died to the law through Christ to belong to the risen One and serve in the new way of the Spirit.

units.label: The law binds only during life

verses.text: Do you not know, brothers (for I am speaking to those who know the law), that the {{nomos|law}} has authority over a man only as long as he lives?

units.label: The marriage analogy
units.note: a widow released to marry another

verses.text: For instance, a married woman is bound by law to her husband as long as he lives. But if her husband dies, she is released from the law of marriage.

So then, if she is joined to another man while her husband is still alive, she is called an adulteress; but if her husband dies, she is free from that law and is not an adulteress if she marries another man.

units.label: Released to belong to another
units.note: died to the law to serve in the new way of the Spirit

verses.text: Therefore, my brothers, you also died to the law through the body of Christ, that you might belong to another, to Him who was raised from the dead, in order that we might bear fruit to God.
For when we lived according to the {{sarx|flesh}}, the sinful passions aroused by the law were at work in our bodies, bearing fruit for death.
But now, having died to what bound us, we have been released from the law, so that we serve in the new way of the {{pneuma|Spirit}}, and not in the old way of the {{gramma|written code}}.

nomos.gloss: Law, especially the law of Moses with its commands. Paul argues that the law exercises its binding authority over a person only during his lifetime. It is holy and good, but it cannot give life or free from sin; the believer's relationship to it is fundamentally changed through death with Christ, so that it no longer stands as the regime under which they live.

sarx.gloss: Flesh, here not merely the body but human nature in its weakness and hostility to God, the old sphere of existence apart from the Spirit. When we lived in the flesh, the law, though good, only stirred up sinful passions that bore fruit for death. The flesh is the realm from which believers have been rescued into the new life of the Spirit.

pneuma.gloss: Spirit, the Holy Spirit, who marks the new age and the new way of serving God. Believers now serve in the new way of the Spirit, a service that flows from inward life and power rather than mere external command. The Spirit is the great gift of the new covenant, writing God's will on the heart and enabling obedience from within.

gramma.gloss: The written code or letter, the law as external written command. The old way of the letter could direct and condemn but could not empower obedience or give life. Paul contrasts it with the new way of the Spirit: not that the law was bad, but that the letter without the Spirit only exposed and provoked sin. The new covenant supplies what the letter could not.

basic.context: Paul has shown that believers died to sin and were freed to serve God. Now he asks about the law. Speaking to people who know the law, he reminds them that a law binds a person only while he is alive. Death ends its claim. He illustrates with marriage: a wife is bound to her husband until he dies, and then she is free to marry another.
basic.hermeneutics: The marriage picture is an analogy, not an allegory to be pressed at every point. Its single point is that death dissolves the binding of the law. Then Paul applies it: believers have died, through the body of Christ, so they are released from the law to belong to the risen Christ. Read verse 4 as the heart of the passage: a change of husbands, from the law to Christ.
basic.originalLanguages: The passage turns on nomos, the law, which binds only during life. When we lived in the sarx, the flesh, the law stirred up sinful passions bearing fruit for death. But now we serve in the new way of the pneuma, the Spirit, not the old way of the gramma, the written code, the letter that could command but not give life.
basic.typology: The marriage bond points to the deeper union between Christ and His people, the true bridegroom to whom the church is now joined. The old covenant, given in written commands, gives way to the new covenant of the Spirit, which the prophets foretold, when God would write His law on the heart and put His Spirit within His people.
basic.christ: Believers are released from the law through the body of Christ, that is, through His crucified body offered in death. They now belong to another, to Him who was raised from the dead. Christ is the new husband to whom the church is joined, the risen Lord in whose life they now bear fruit to God. Union with Him, not the law, is the source of their new obedience.
basic.god: The whole aim of this release is that we might bear fruit to God. God is the one served in the new way of the Spirit, and the fruit of the new marriage to Christ is fruit for Him. God has provided in Christ and by the Spirit what the law could never supply, life and the power to obey from the heart.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 6 grounds this in dying and rising with Christ. Galatians 2 says through the law I died to the law so that I might live to God. 2 Corinthians 3 contrasts the letter that kills with the Spirit that gives life. Jeremiah 31 promises the new covenant written on the heart.
basic.oneStory: The Bible moves from the law given at Sinai on tablets of stone to the new covenant promised by the prophets, when God would put His Spirit within His people. Here that turning is announced: believers, having died with Christ, are released from the old regime of the written law and joined to the risen Christ, serving God in the new way of the Spirit, and bearing fruit for Him.

context.literary:
Romans 7:1-6 is a bridge. It looks back to chapter 6, where Paul has said twice that believers are no longer under law but under grace, 6:14 and 6:15, and it opens the way to the long defence of the law in 7:7-25 and the Spirit chapter of Romans 8. Verses 5 and 6 are the hinge, for the first sets out the old life that 7:7-25 will analyse, sinful passions aroused by the law, and the second announces the Spirit, whom Paul will unfold from 8:1.

Within the section the argument is built in three steps that are each marked by a small word. Verse 1 asks a question that expects the answer yes, then states a principle. Verses 2 and 3 apply the principle to marriage with a careful 'if... but if' pattern, two cases of a wife and her husband, one in which he is alive and she is bound, the other in which he is dead and she is free. Verse 4 begins 'Therefore', and applies it to the readers, and verses 5 and 6 explain with 'for' and 'but now'. The purpose clauses stack up: 'that you might belong to another', 'in order that we might bear fruit to God', 'so that we serve in the new way of the Spirit'.

Paul shifts pronouns with care. In verse 4 he says 'you died' and then 'we might bear fruit', and from verse 5 on he speaks as 'we', including himself in the story of life in the flesh. The two fruit-bearings are set beside each other with the same verb, 'bear fruit to God' in verse 4 and 'bearing fruit for death' in verse 5, so that the fruit of the old life and the fruit of the new are the two possible harvests of one body. The imagery picks up the harvests of 6:21 and 6:22 and moves the argument from a master to a marriage.
context.historical:
Marriage law is a good choice of illustration because it was understood everywhere. In Israel a woman who joined herself to another man while her husband lived committed adultery, Leviticus 20:10, though a husband could dismiss his wife by a written certificate, Deuteronomy 24:1-2. Roman law was more permissive about divorce, but in every system death ended a marriage cleanly and left the survivor free to marry. Paul states the principle as plainly as he does the same truth in 1 Corinthians 7:39, and he can assume agreement from Jewish and Gentile readers alike. Later rabbinic writings record the saying that a person who has died is free from the commandments, which suggests that the idea that law ends at death was not strange to Jewish thought.

The question of the law was a live one in Rome. The congregation had Jewish believers who had been expelled and had come back and Gentile believers who had grown in their absence, and by the end of the letter we find them divided over food and days, Romans 14:1-3. Paul had to explain how a church that no longer lives under the Mosaic regime can still honour the Scriptures. The phrase 'those who know the law' tells us that Paul counted his readers as people familiar with the Old Testament.

Verse 6 also touches an Old Testament picture of Israel as the LORD's wife. The prophets spoke of the LORD as Israel's husband, Isaiah 54:5, and Jeremiah, speaking of the new covenant, recalled a covenant that Israel broke 'though I was a husband to them', Jeremiah 31:32. Paul's readers, steeped in that language, would hear the marriage metaphor against a background of covenant faithfulness and unfaithfulness, and the written code of Sinai set against the Spirit of the new covenant.
context.canonical:
The passage belongs to a thread that runs from the prophets to the end of the New Testament. Jeremiah 31:31-34 promises a new covenant, not like the one broken at the exodus, in which God puts His law in the mind and inscribes it on the heart. Ezekiel 36:26-27 adds that God will give a new heart and put His Spirit within His people to cause them to walk in His statutes. Romans 7:6, with its 'new way of the Spirit', is Paul announcing that those promises have arrived.

Paul's other letters take up the same teaching in different forms. In 2 Corinthians 3:6 he calls himself a minister of a new covenant, 'not of the letter but of the Spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life'. Galatians 2:19 says, 'through the law I died to the law so that I might live to God', and Galatians 3:23-25 describes the law as a guardian until Christ came. Colossians 2:14 says the written decrees that stood against us have been nailed to the cross. Romans 10:4 says Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes, and Hebrews 8:13 says the first covenant has become obsolete. Against this stands Matthew 5:17, where Jesus says He came not to abolish the Law but to fulfil it, which keeps the whole body of teaching honest: what is ended is the law's rule over the believer, not the law's testimony to God.

The marriage thread continues in the New Testament. Ephesians 5:25-32 reads marriage as a picture of Christ and the church, 2 Corinthians 11:2 speaks of presenting the church as a pure virgin to one husband, and Revelation 19:7 looks forward to the marriage of the Lamb.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul had to answer a charge in advance. If believers are not under law, are they not lawless? In chapter 6 he answered with ownership. Here he answers with a different point, that the whole system by which the law held people has been left behind by a death. His aim is not to criticize the law but to say what has happened to the believer. The law remains what it was; it is the person's relationship to it that has altered.

He meant the Romans to see that their new life is not a lesser form of the old. They are not moving from strict rules to loose ones, but from one realm to another, from a union that produced fruit for death to a union that produces fruit for God. The word 'belong' in verse 4 is the key. Their obedience is no longer a rule imposed from outside, it is the life of a person joined to another person.

He also meant to prepare the ground for what follows. Having said that the law aroused sinful passions, verse 5, he knew the Romans might conclude that the law is the culprit. So the passage ends with an open question that Paul takes up at once in verse 7, and the careful reader is meant to hear the gentle tone with which he turns the argument, not against the law but against the flesh.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Verses 1 to 3 give a general principle about law and marriage, and nothing in them is a command to be applied to marriage today. Paul is not teaching on divorce or remarriage here, for that is the business of other passages such as 1 Corinthians 7 and Matthew 19. He borrows the commonly known truth about marriage to illustrate a different point about law. Treating the passage as a marriage manual misreads the aim.

Verses 4 to 6 describe what has happened to believers. They died, they have been released, they now belong to Christ. No command appears in these verses at all. The purpose, bearing fruit to God and serving in the new way of the Spirit, is stated as the goal of the release, not as a task that earns it. That has a practical bearing on how Christians live. Obedience is not a rule that becomes bearable once we have strengthened our will. It is the life of a person who has been given a new partner and a new power.

The verses also invite a warning. Paul describes life in the flesh as one where the law arouses the sinful passions. It does not follow that a person who feels the pull of sin is therefore under law, or that the Spirit will remove temptation. The passage describes a different standing, not a life free of conflict, and Paul will go on to show in 7:14-25 and 8:13 that believers still fight.

debates.question: Who are 'those who know the law', and does the section address Jewish believers only?

views.label: Jewish Christians especially
views.case: The phrase 'those who know the law' looks most natural of people raised on the Torah, and the problem Paul tackles, whether the law still binds, would be most urgent for them. Jewish believers had returned to Rome after the expulsion under Claudius, Acts 18:2, and they would have felt the question most sharply.

views.label: The whole church, Jew and Gentile
views.case: Paul calls them 'brothers' and has addressed the whole congregation since chapter 1. Gentile believers who had learned the Scriptures in the synagogue or in the church knew the law too, and Paul can say in Romans 6:14 and 7:4 that 'you' are no longer under it. On this view 'the law' is the Torah as the church reads it, known to all.

views.label: Anyone who understands how law works
views.case: A smaller group takes the phrase to include Gentiles who knew the principle behind any law, that its claims end at death. The marriage illustration would then work for readers from every background, since it rests on a principle held by Jewish and Roman law alike.

debates.bearing: Paul's second person in verse 4 and first person plural in the rest of the section shows he means the entire church. Whatever their background, all believers share the same death and the same new husband, which fits the letter's larger aim of one family from Jews and Gentiles, Romans 15:5-7.

debates.question: Whose death sets the believer free, and who is the husband in the illustration?

views.label: The believer dies, the law is the husband
views.case: Verse 4 says 'you also died to the law', so the party who dies is the believer. The law is then the old husband and the risen Christ is the new. The picture is slightly awkward because the wife in the illustration is freed by her husband's death, yet here it is the wife who dies. Paul seems content with the awkwardness, since his aim is to establish that death ends the claim.

views.label: The old self is the husband
views.case: Others note that Paul never says the law dies and prefer to see the first husband as the old self in Adam, crucified with Christ, Romans 6:6. The law is then the jurisdiction that bound the marriage, and when the old self dies the marriage is over. This reading keeps the law intact, as Paul does in 7:12.

views.label: The illustration should not be pressed
views.case: Many interpreters think Paul is deliberately not allegorizing. The point of verses 2 and 3 is only that law holds only for a lifetime; verse 4 then applies that point in a fresh way. Looking for an exact correspondent for each figure goes beyond what the passage supplies.

debates.bearing: All three readings agree that a death has occurred, that it is the believer's, and that it has been through Christ. The text puts weight on this and not on the identity of the first husband, so the safest course is to hold the picture loosely and the conclusion firmly.

debates.question: How far should the marriage analogy be pressed?

views.label: It makes one main point, that death dissolves the law's binding
views.case: The historic reading takes the analogy as illustrating a single truth: as death frees a widow to remarry, so death with Christ frees the believer from the law to belong to another; the details are not to be allegorized.

views.label: Every element must correspond precisely
views.case: Some try to match each figure exactly, asking who dies and who remarries; but Paul mixes the roles, since in verse 4 the believers themselves die, showing the analogy is meant to teach one truth, not a strict allegory.

debates.bearing: Reading it for its single point keeps the focus where Paul places it: through death with Christ the believer is lawfully released from the old regime and freely joined to the risen Lord to bear fruit to God.

debates.question: Does released from the law mean the law has no place at all for believers?

views.label: Freedom from the law as a covenant regime, not from all moral instruction
views.case: The historic Reformed reading holds that believers are freed from the law as a covenant of works and condemnation, yet the law still instructs and guides the Christian life, now written on the heart by the Spirit.

views.label: Complete abolition of the law in every sense
views.case: Some read it as the total abrogation of the law; but Paul immediately insists the law is holy, righteous, and good, so the release is from its condemning and provoking role, not from its abiding revelation of God's will.

debates.bearing: Distinguishing the law as covenant regime from the law as revelation of God's will guards both grace and holiness: the believer is free from condemnation yet serves God's good will in the power of the Spirit.

study.originalLanguages:
The first verb to notice is the one translated 'has authority' in verse 1, kurieuo, 'to be lord over'. Paul used the very same verb in 6:9 when he said death no longer has mastery over Christ, and again in 6:14 when he said that sin shall not be master over believers. Placing the law in the same sentence structure marks it out as a third power with a claim on the person, alongside sin and death, and it explains why freedom from one of them needs freedom from the others. It does not make the law evil. It says the law, in its regime, rules over those who are under it, and that the rule has a time limit.

The verb 'released' in verses 2 and 6 is katargeo, which means to render inoperative or to bring to nothing. The wife is 'released from the law of marriage', and believers are 'released from the law'. The same verb was used in 6:6 of the body of sin being rendered powerless, and in 3:31 Paul asked whether faith 'nullifies' the law and answered no. The comparison is instructive. The law is not nullified, it stays in force as God's word; what has been rendered inoperative is its hold over those who have died. A person is released from the law's jurisdiction without the law being repealed.

The tense and voice of verse 4 deserve attention. 'You died' is a passive, ethanatothete, literally 'you were put to death', as though the death were done to the believers in union with Christ and not by their own effort. The related verb thanatoo comes back in 8:13 in the active form, 'you put to death the deeds of the body', so that the passive of chapter 7 and the active of chapter 8 are the two sides of one reality, what has been done for us and what we now do by the Spirit.

Verse 6 speaks of 'the new way of the Spirit' and 'the old way of the written code'. Literally these are newness of Spirit and oldness of letter, kainotes pneumatos and palaiotes grammatos, a pairing that recalls 2 Corinthians 3:6 and the 'newness of life' of 6:4. Gramma, the written code, does not mean that Scripture is dead. It names the law as a written demand without the power to produce what it asks, set against the Spirit who supplies it.

In verse 5 'in the flesh' is Paul's phrase for the whole condition of life before and apart from Christ, and not merely for the physical body. The Greek idiom is 'to be in the flesh', and he reverses it in 8:9, 'you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit'. It describes a realm or an age. The 'sinful passions' are literally the passions of sins, pathemata ton hamartion, aroused 'through the law' and 'at work', energeito, in the bodily members. The word for members, melos, is the same one that stood behind the 'parts of your body' offered to God in 6:13 and 6:19, so that the body which was to be an instrument of righteousness had been the workshop of the passions.

typology.type: The marriage bond, human and divine
typology.fulfillment: The prophets used marriage as the picture of the covenant, with the LORD as Israel's husband, Isaiah 54:5, and Hosea 2:16 promising that Israel would one day call Him 'my Husband' and no longer 'my Master'. Paul here lets the picture stretch further: the believer is joined, by a death, to the risen Christ, and Ephesians 5:25-32 reads marriage itself as a sign of Christ and the church. The correspondence is not exact, since in Romans 7 the first partner is a regime and not a person, and the picture runs out at that point. What it conveys is the intimate loyalty of a bride, the glad belonging that the marriage of the Lamb will complete, Revelation 19:7.

typology.type: The covenant written on stone and the covenant written within
typology.fulfillment: At Sinai God wrote the covenant words on tablets of stone, Exodus 34:28, and the people accepted them as a written code. Jeremiah 31:33 promised a covenant written on the heart, and Paul says that the Corinthians are a letter from Christ written 'not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts', 2 Corinthians 3:3. In Romans 7:6 the old way of the written code gives way to the new way of the Spirit. The type falls short of being a rival, for the same God spoke both; the stone was a faithful witness, but only the Spirit could write what the stone demanded.

The widow who is free to marry, verse 3, is not a prophecy of anything in particular, but it illustrates a pattern Paul finds again and again, that only a death can open a new relationship. Christ's death dealt with the claim that stood against us, Colossians 2:14, and Galatians 3:13 says He redeemed us from the curse of the law. In Christ the release is more than legal: it comes with a resurrection and a new partner, so that the widow is not left alone but belongs to One who is alive. The picture falls short because a widow's first husband stays dead, whereas the One to whom believers now belong lives forever, Romans 6:9-10.

typology.type: Fruit for the owner of the field
typology.fulfillment: The vineyard and the fruitful tree are among the oldest pictures of Israel's calling, Isaiah 5:1-7, and the demand that Israel bear fruit for the LORD runs through the prophets. Jesus gathered it up in John 15:5, 'apart from Me you can do nothing', and Paul draws the same thread in Romans 7:4, 'in order that we might bear fruit to God'. The type shows that fruitfulness is the purpose of the covenant, and it finds its fulfilment in a people joined to the true Vine. It falls short where Israel's vine bore wild grapes, Isaiah 5:4, for the fruit of the new union is produced by the life of the One to whom the branches are joined.

study.christ:
The passage rests on the phrase 'through the body of Christ'. The body is His crucified body, the same flesh and blood that Colossians 1:22 says reconciles us 'through death', and that 1 Peter 2:24 says bore our sins on the tree, 'so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness'. Hebrews 10:10 adds that we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all. When Paul says believers died to the law through that body, he means that Christ's death was not only for us but also counts as ours, so that all that the law could demand of a sinner has been laid on Him, and the person who is in Him has gone through that death with Him. The law's claim has not been argued away. It has been satisfied.

The passage leads to Christ by the person to whom we are joined. 'To Him who was raised from the dead' is a deliberate phrase. The new union is with a living Lord, one who in His death dealt with the old claim and in His resurrection is the new life. Romans 14:9 says He died and returned to life that He might be Lord of both the dead and the living. The word 'another' reminds us that the believer's new husband is not a rival to the first but the one in whom the first's claims were exhausted. Galatians 2:20 puts it in the first person: 'I have been crucified with Christ, and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me.'

It leads to Christ by the theme of fulfilment. Matthew 5:17 says He came to fulfil the law, and Galatians 4:4 says He was born under the law to redeem those under it. His whole life was lived under the law's claim without a failure, so that He could take its curse, Galatians 3:13, and give its righteousness, Romans 8:4. Romans 10:4 says He is the end of the law to bring righteousness to everyone who believes, and 'end' there carries both senses, goal and conclusion.

It leads to Christ by the picture of the bridegroom. John the Baptist said that the bride belongs to the bridegroom, John 3:29, and Jesus spoke of Himself as a bridegroom who would be taken away, Mark 2:19-20, which He did in His death. Paul's own concern for the Corinthians was to present them as a pure bride to one husband, 2 Corinthians 11:2, and Ephesians 5:25-27 describes Christ giving Himself up for the church to present her holy and blameless.

A caution keeps the reading honest. In Paul's own illustration the first husband dies and a new husband is chosen, and he does not say the law died or that Christ replaced the law as a rival husband. Allegorizing every figure would put words in his mouth. What the text establishes is the substantial truth that a death, the death of Christ in which believers share, ends the law's claim, and a resurrection opens a living relationship.
study.god:
The passage shows God as a God who keeps His word and still does a new thing. The law is His, and Paul does not hint at a change of mind. Yet it was always a stage. God had promised through Jeremiah that He would make a new covenant, Jeremiah 31:31, and the sentence of Romans 7:6 is that promise arriving. He is faithful to the old and faithful to the promise of the new, and He keeps both by the one death of His Son. The apparent tension between a God who gave the law and a God who releases from it is resolved because the release does not contradict the law. The law's sentence on sin was carried out, and so those who share in the death are free of a claim that has been settled.

He is a God who raises the dead. The new relationship is with Him 'who was raised from the dead', and the Father's act of raising is what makes the new life possible. The same power is at work in the believer, as Romans 8:11 will say. God is therefore not only a lawgiver, He is a life-giver, and the gift of the Spirit is the means of that life being lived, 'in the new way of the Spirit'.

He is a God who desires fruit, and the fruit is 'to God'. This is more than an agricultural image. It says that the point of the believer's life is a life offered back to Him, and it shows God as the one who is glad in what is produced in His people. It also shows that the fruit He wants is the fruit of a union and not the output of a rulebook. The Father delights in children who look like the Son by the Spirit.

He is a God of covenant faithfulness who is also a bridegroom. The prophets spoke of the LORD as Israel's husband and were bitter at Israel's unfaithfulness. Paul's reading is that the bridegroom has come in the flesh and has bought a bride by dying for her. The language is of love and not just authority. For worship, this passage teaches that obedience is a love-response to a Saviour who has given Himself, and that the heart's proper posture is not the cringing of someone under a law but the gladness of someone who belongs.

The three persons are at work. The Son's body was given, the Father raised Him, and the Spirit gives the new way of life. Paul does not argue for the Trinity here, but he assumes it in the way he describes the believer's new life.

crossReferences.note: Paul has already said sin shall not be master, because believers are not under law but under grace. Romans 7:1-6 explains how that freedom came about: by a death that ends the law's jurisdiction, so that being under grace is not a legal fiction but a changed standing.

Paul asks whether faith nullifies the law and answers that it upholds it. The same verb, katargeo, appears in 7:2 and 7:6 of being released from the law, and the two together mean that the believer is freed from the law's jurisdiction while the law itself stands as God's word.

Paul states the same marriage principle, that a wife is bound as long as her husband lives and is free when he dies. It shows that the illustration is not a special argument invented for Romans 7 but a commonplace which Paul uses for his own purposes.

Paul calls himself a minister of a new covenant, and sets the written code against the Spirit in nearly the words that close Romans 7:6. The two passages interpret each other: the written code is the law as bare demand, and the Spirit is the same law received with the power to be lived.

Through the law Paul died to the law, so that he might live to God, crucified with Christ and indwelt by Him. It is the autobiographical version of Romans 7:4, with the same logic of a death that opens a life and the same sense that the life lived now belongs to Christ.

God promises a new covenant unlike the one broken after the exodus, with His law put in the mind and written on the heart. The promise underlies the whole passage and shows why Paul calls the change 'the new way of the Spirit', not a departure from God's plan.

God promises a new heart and His own Spirit within His people, to cause them to walk in His statutes. This shows that the law's demands are not discarded; the Spirit makes possible the obedience that the written code could only require.

Paul's answer to this section is only a chapter away. The law of the Spirit of life has set believers free, and what the law could not do God did by sending His Son, so that the righteous standard of the law might be fulfilled in those who walk by the Spirit.

Christ gave Himself up for the church to make her holy and blameless. Here the marriage image is taken in the direction of Christ's love for His bride, showing what the new husband of Romans 7:4 has done to bring her to Himself.

God cancelled the debt that stood against us, nailing it to the cross. It explains how a death can release from the law's claim: the written record of what was owed has been dealt with at the cross, so that no one in Christ remains bound to the old account.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a relationship before it has any law. In Eden there was one prohibition and a whole garden of freedom, and the man and woman walked with God. The law as the Old Testament knows it arrives with Israel at Sinai, four hundred and thirty years after the promise to Abraham, Galatians 3:17, and it is given to a people already redeemed from Egypt. It is God's own word, setting out what life with Him looks like, and it exposes the sin of those who receive it.

The prophets show that the law could not by itself change the human heart. Israel broke the covenant, and Jeremiah calls it a covenant that was broken though the LORD had been Israel's husband, Jeremiah 31:32. That is why the same prophets promise something new, a covenant in which God Himself would write the law within His people and put His Spirit inside them, Jeremiah 31:33 and Ezekiel 36:27. The long story of Israel's failure is therefore not an embarrassment for the law but the setting for the promise that God would do what the law could only ask.

Romans 7:1-6 is the point where that promise is announced as kept. Christ has died, and those who are in Him died with Him; Christ has been raised, and they now belong to the Risen One. The Old Testament longing for a heart that would obey is answered not by a better code but by a new union. The people of God are no longer defined by the written regime of Sinai but by the Spirit of the Lord, 2 Corinthians 3:17.

The story does not stop at the church's present experience. The marriage image looks ahead to its end, for Scripture closes with the wedding of the Lamb and a bride who has made herself ready, Revelation 19:7, and the new Jerusalem is described as a bride adorned for her husband, Revelation 21:2. The ultimate fruit to God is a people in whose hearts the law is written and who see His face. What Romans 7:4 calls bearing fruit to God will be complete when the bride is finally presented in glory and the longing that began in Eden, to dwell with God without shame, is satisfied in the city where God's own presence is the temple.

quiz.q: What principle does Paul state about the law in verse 1?

options.text: The law has authority over a person only as long as he lives.
options.note: Death ends the law's binding claim, the key to the argument.

options.text: The law has authority over a person forever, even after death.
options.note: Paul says the opposite; death dissolves the law's authority.

options.text: The law never had any real authority at all.
options.note: The law is holy and had genuine authority; its claim simply ends at death.

options.text: The law binds only those who choose to accept it.
options.note: It rightly senses the law's claim is not permanent, but it is death, not personal choice, that ends the law's authority.

quiz.q: What is the single point of the marriage analogy?

options.text: Death dissolves the binding of the law, freeing one to belong to another.
options.note: As a widow is free to remarry, so death with Christ frees the believer.

options.text: That remarriage is always sinful.
options.note: Paul says the widow may remarry without sin; that is the point of freedom.

options.text: That every detail of marriage must match the law exactly.
options.note: The analogy does concern the law, but it makes one main point and is not a strict allegory to be pressed at every detail.

options.text: That the law is like a cruel husband to be escaped.
options.note: The law is holy; the point is release through death, not that the law is cruel.

quiz.q: How were believers released from the law, according to verse 4?

options.text: They died to the law through the body of Christ.
options.note: Through Christ's crucified body they died and were freed.

options.text: They simply decided the law no longer applied to them.
options.note: Believers are indeed free from the law, but by dying with Christ, not by their own decision that it no longer applies.

options.text: They kept the law perfectly and so graduated from it.
options.note: No one keeps the law perfectly; release is through Christ's death.

options.text: The law was abolished so that righteousness no longer matters.
options.note: The aim is to bear fruit to God, not to abandon righteousness.

quiz.q: To whom are believers joined after being released from the law?

options.text: To Christ, who was raised from the dead, so as to bear fruit to God.
options.note: The believer belongs to the risen Christ, the new bridegroom.

options.text: To no one; they now belong only to themselves.
options.note: They are joined to Christ, not left autonomous.

options.text: To a stricter version of the law.
options.note: They are joined to the risen Christ, not to a new law regime.

options.text: To the Spirit as a replacement for Christ.
options.note: Believers do serve in the new way of the Spirit, but they are joined to the risen Christ Himself, not to the Spirit as a replacement for Him.

quiz.q: What is the new way in which believers now serve God?

options.text: In the new way of the Spirit, not the old way of the written code.
options.note: The Spirit gives inward life the letter could not supply.

options.text: In the old way of the written code, kept more carefully.
options.note: This still values God's commands, but Paul contrasts the new way of the Spirit with the old way of the letter, not merely a more careful letter keeping.

options.text: By ignoring God's will altogether.
options.note: The new way bears fruit to God; it does not ignore His will.

options.text: By a private spirituality with no reference to God.
options.note: Serving in the Spirit is service to God, bearing fruit for Him.

questions: Paul says the law binds a person only during life, and believers have died with Christ. How does knowing you are released from the law as a way of acceptance change how you relate to God?
The believer is joined to the risen Christ as a bride to a husband. What does it mean for your daily life to belong to Christ rather than to the law?
Under the flesh, even the good law only stirred up sin and bore fruit for death. Where have you experienced that mere rules cannot change the heart?
The purpose of our release is to bear fruit to God. What kind of fruit is God looking for from your union with Christ?
We now serve in the new way of the Spirit, not the old way of the letter. What would it look like this week to obey from the Spirit's inward power rather than external duty alone?

translationNotes.note: Speaking to those who know the law addresses readers familiar with the Scriptures, both Jewish believers and Gentiles who knew them; the principle that law binds only during life was common to both Jewish and Roman legal thought.
Through the body of Christ refers to His crucified body offered in death; the believer's death with Christ is the ground of release from the law and of the new belonging to the risen Lord.

The old way of the written code renders the letter, gramma, the external written law; the contrast with the Spirit is not that the law was evil but that the letter could command and condemn while only the Spirit gives life.
